To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the foreign workers in the Luxembourg labor market are more vulnerable to earnings inequality than their Luxembourg counterparts.
the foreign share of employment in the Luxembourg economy has been increasing since the 1960s.

1) the earnings distribution of native-born workers is more compressed than that of foreign-born workers, 2) the earnings of native-born workers are more stable than those of foreign-born workers over time and across cohorts, and 3) the earnings of the native-born workers have become more compressed over time while the earnings of foreign-born workers have become less compressed.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the dynamics of the earnings distribution, the role of foreign workers in the earnings inequality trends, the role of earnings inequality in the wage distribution and the impact of foreign workers on the wage distribution in Luxembourg between 1988 and 2009.

the following issues: 1) the impact of the foreign population in the labour force on earnings inequality; 2) the impact of earnings dynamics on earnings inequality and the role played by the foreign population; and 3) the impact of foreign population on earnings dynamics and earnings inequality.
the following issues: How do earnings inequality and mobility evolve over time?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of this study are mixed.
the model is a very good fit to the data and the results are very robust to different model specifications.
the model is able to capture the main trends and patterns in the Luxembourg labour market, but that the results are not always as expected.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the foreign population has contributed to the rise in earnings inequality in Luxembourg in the last two decades.
the foreign worker population in Luxembourg is not homogeneous, but rather is composed of different groups of workers.

foreign workers are more likely to have lower earnings and to experience more earnings instability than Luxembourgish workers, and that the earnings inequality among Luxembourgish workers increased between 1988 and 2009.
The main takeaway from our work is that
foreign workers have contributed significantly to the increase of earnings inequality in Luxembourg over the past two decades.
the dynamics of earnings inequality in Luxembourg are largely driven by the dynamics of earnings of the foreign population.
the earnings distribution in Luxembourg is highly sensitive to the presence of foreign workers.
